 O R D E R

The accused in C.C. No.378 of 2003 on the files of the court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class -11, Perinthalmanna, filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16 (1A)(i) read with Section 2(ia)(j) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short 'the PFAAct').
2.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class -11, Perinthalmanna
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Heard.

3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 4.7.2002 at about 12.30 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector, purchased 750 grams of green grams (cherupayar parippu), from the revision petitioner.
After complying with the legal formalities, one sample was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.
The Public Analyst filed Ext. P13 report, which would show that the sample contained synthetic food colour tartarzine and hence, the sample was adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW3 were examined and Exts.P1 to P19 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 and D2 were marked on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has argued that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P13 report of the Public Analyst cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 6 It was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The Division Bench of this Court in Rasheed v. Food Inspector [2016 (2) KLT 390] considered the above question on a reference by a learned Single Judge.

The Division Bench in Rasheed (supra) held that if an analysis is required to initiate prosecution, there should be notified laboratory and validated method of A.Hussain S/O. Ahammad Kutty vs The Food Inspector on 20 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/136142995/
2 analysis as mandated under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act for a successful prosecution as held by the Apex Court in Pepsico Holdings (supra).
7.

entities.text: A.Hussain S/O. Ahammad Kutty vs The Food Inspector on 20 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)
(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P13 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).
Therefore, the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1A) (i) read with Section 2(ia)(j) of PFA Act, 1954 , cannot be sustained.

In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the Courts below under Section 16 (1A)(i) read with Section 2 (ia)(j) of the P.F.A. Act and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bond of the revision petitioner stands cancelled and he is set at liberty.
